transcript: If you pay for Claude, ChatGPT, or any other AI service, you are wasting your money unless you have agents running while you sleep. This is Overnight Agent Workflows 101, and by the end of this video, you should have an idea of how to have AI complete tasks while you're away doing other things. To establish credibility, here's my AI usage in the last 30 days, and the money that comes out of my pocket is only $200 a month to Anthropic. So, I run a startup and all the things associated with the startup, code to review, marketing to do, videos to post, and last night before bed, I gave it the prompt, what can you do overnight that's actually useful and doesn't need me. And here's how to set up your workflow so it's that easy for you too. Number one, define the task and scope clearly before you start. It's like any other human you talk to. You can't just tell them to do something when they don't know what you want them to do. Or in my case last night, it had a list of GitHub issues to work through. Number two, give every sub agent its own copy of the project. If you want things to happen in parallel, have your Claude tell you about Git work trees. Number three, baby proof your project. You've heard all the horror stories of on-call engineers getting pinged at 3am because the database got deleted by the agents. Only give it the permissions that it needs and take away all the dangerous buttons. Cloud Code has a feature called hooks that blocks a command before it runs. For example, in my startup, agents can't merge code, can't post to GitHub, and can't push to my live database. And trust me, you will sleep a lot easier when you know that no matter how bad the AI messes up, at least it's reversible. Number four, have other agents check the work. You can have recursive loops of design, build, test, review from different agents going back and forth so that you don't wake up to a lot of code that is complete and utter bullcrap. You will wake up to bullcrap that has been reviewed by at least a couple other agents. Number five, make the deliverables either something clean and defined or decisions that you have to make once you wake up in the morning. For example, my morning report was seven questions that I answered in one line each. So if you're paying for AI and it's just sitting there while you sleep, that's just like a gym membership you never use. That was day 88 of posting every day into my dating app as 3000 daily active users. Follow along for the journey. Peace.

transcript: I am a meat proxy between the real world and my AI agents, and until today I was wasting way more time than I needed to. So here is something that 6 billion tokens taught me. For some context, I've been vibe coding pretty seriously since around June, and over time I've been giving my agents more and more control over my code base. Earlier this month, I gave Fable basically full autonomy, and then I wake up one morning and see that 20 pull requests got force merged and it messed up a lot of stuff. My immediate response was to put a trillion rule set and branch protections on all the important stuff and make sure that me and at least one other human reviewed every change. This made my system very safe, very controlled, but oh so slow and frustrating to change. And this weekend, I was at a hackathon where my entire mindset changed. I had agents watching my test screen recordings and writing GitHub issues and other agents spitting up sub-agent for each issue and more sub-agents reviewing those solutions. We were shipping a new test flight build every 30 minutes. Every single build, more and more stuff was getting fixed. Constant loops, lots of token spend, but oh so jaw dropping results. And it was all because my roommate, who by the way burned 13 billion tokens that weekend, told me, and I quote, Dude, you have to trust your agents more. And it all clicked. transcript: This is what nobody seems to understand about AI agents, but LLMs by themselves can't actually do anything. People confuse all the parts and I'm tired of explaining it, so here's a basic overview of how AI agents actually work. Why should you trust anything that I say? That's up to you, but I use a lot of AI and I study computer science at a decent program. So the first part of any AI agent is, of course, the brain. The brain is a large language model. This is your Claude Opus 5.5, your DeepSeek V4, your GPT-Astra, and all a large language model does is predict what comes next, one token at a time. A token is basically a chunk of a word around four characters. The brain has what's known as a context window, and this is basically the brain's notepad. It's everything it can see and remember right now. For most of the big models at the moment, that's around a million tokens, and for reference, that's about one and a half copies of the entire Lord of the Rings trilogy. Now we get to the fancy stuff, and this is why AI can actually do stuff now. The harness. If we think about our own brain, by itself, it can't do anything. It takes in electrical signals and puts out electrical signals. Now imagine we attached a nervous system and gave it hands. Now it can actually do some stuff. The harness is the LLM's hands. It lets it read files, run commands, search the web, edit files, all that fancy stuff. And better harnesses are part of the reason why AI can do math now instead of just guessing numbers that look right like how it was a couple years ago. And that is, to put it simply, what an agent is. A brain with a context window with hands that can use tools going back and forth until whatever job you gave it is done. Then, in November 2024, Anthropic gave agents a way to ask someone else's hands to do things called Model Context Protocol, or MCP. This lets your AI connect to stuff like your calendar, or your email, or your Google Drive, things that live outside the agent. And all of this is packaged into the app that you download. This is your codex window or cloud code terminal. You never talk to the agent directly. You talk to the app that houses it. Well, that's not in the window. You talk to the app that houses it. And hopefully, that's a good enough high-level overview of what an agent is. This is super simplified, and I skimmed over a lot of details, but at least now people will stop calling their vibe-coded GPT wrapper startup a harness. And speaking of vibe-coded GPT wrapper startups, that was day 89 of posting every day until mine has 3,000 daily active users. Follow along for the journey. Peace.

transcript: If you are building anything, this is the only number that you should care about. It's called the net promoter score. How it works is you ask your customers one question. How likely are you to recommend this to a friend on a scale from 0 to 10? A score of 0 through 6 counts as a minus 1, 7 or 8 counts as a 0, and 9 or 10 counts as a plus 1. You add it all up and you'll land somewhere between negative 100 and positive 100. It's one of the more brutal metrics, but that's exactly why it's so effective. For example, Uber. They completely reshape transportation. They have a positive 30 out of 100. Another example, I'm building a dating app. The numbers in this industry are absolute dog water. There was a study done in 2024 by a research firm called Measuring U. They ran this test on seven of the big boys. Every single one came back negative. The best scoring one was match at negative seven. The worst was hinge at negative 45. Designed to be deleted, they say. I'm kind of a little bit of BS. Now, sure, the industry that it's in messes up the question and the metrics might get skewed, but negative 45 can't just be a measurement problem. That's probably people just being genuinely unhappy. Moral of the story, if you're playing the long-term game, you should focus on happy customers as opposed to short-term profit because business becomes easier when you have a product that sells itself. Thank you.

transcript: I reverse engineered Tinder and here are the top three things that I found. So there's a GitHub repo blown up right now called reverse engineer anything. It has basically made all software as a service obsolete. I decided to play around with it and have it look at Tinder. Quick disclaimer, their actual algorithm lives on their servers and hacking is illegal. All this information is from the user facing binary. You've probably heard the rumor that Tinder gives you a secret ELO score for how hot you are. I searched the entire app for ELO. There is one reference to ELO. It is for your Duolingo chess rating. Thing one, the app times you. Every swipe, left or right, sends Tinder how many milliseconds you spent on that profile, how long you looked at each photo, and which photo you were on when you swiped. So when you swipe left on someone but stare at their third photo for like eight seconds, your phone reports that. What do they do with it? I don't know. Thing two. It tracks messages you didn't send. Picture this. It's 1am. You type something that might get you banned. Tinder pops up right before you send. Are you sure? So you tap no. Delete. Character development. The app still sends Tinder what you typed. It's only for messages that set off the safety warning, but still, that message you deleted isn't as deleted as you thought. Thing three. And this is the big one. Tinder has an AI feature you can turn on that scans your camera roll. I was reading through it, and first I found a face recognition engine. It asked, is this you? Then finds your face across up to 3000 of your photos. Then I started seeing the scores it gives every single photo. Some are safety filters, like explicit, but two are called RSRR female and RSRR male. Tinder is publicly ranked things by right swipes received ratio, so I'm fairly sure that's what that stands for. It's basically a score for how many right swipes that photo would get. One version for women, one for men. Picked by the gender on your profile. Then it uploads tiny thumbnails of some of your photos to Tinder. The screen you agreed to says your photos stay private. A different screen says they store select photos.
